chapters.title: What Is a Dinosaur?
chapters.tease: Birds are dinosaurs, pterosaurs are not: one family tree sorts the whole Mesozoic cast.

chapters.title: How a Fossil Forms
chapters.tease: Fossilisation is a long lottery; knowing the odds tells us which dinosaurs we will never see.

chapters.title: Deep Time and the Geological Clock
chapters.tease: Rock layers and radioactive clocks turned a jumble of monsters into a 165-million-year history.

chapters.title: Megalosaurus: The First Named Dinosaur
chapters.tease: The first dinosaur ever named was a meat-eater from an Oxfordshire roofing quarry.

chapters.title: Mary Anning and the Jurassic Coast
chapters.tease: A working-class collector's sea reptiles proved extinction was real and launched palaeontology.

chapters.title: Gideon Mantell and Iguanodon
chapters.tease: Iguanodon was the first plant-eating dinosaur named, and its 'horn' turned out to be a thumb.

chapters.title: Richard Owen and the Crystal Palace Monsters
chapters.tease: Owen coined 'Dinosauria'; Hawkins's statues made the world's first dinosaur craze.

chapters.title: The Bone Wars
chapters.tease: A feud between two rich naturalists filled the world's museums with Jurassic giants.

chapters.title: Trace Fossils: Footprints, Eggs and Dung
chapters.tease: Footprints, nests and dung capture behaviour that no skeleton can show.

chapters.title: New Eyes on Old Bones
chapters.tease: Scanners, microscopes and code now read growth, colour and body heat from bones.

chapters.title: The Great Dying
chapters.tease: The worst extinction in Earth's history cleared the stage on which the archosaurs and dinosaurs rose.

chapters.title: Pangaea
chapters.tease: A single supercontinent let the first dinosaurs walk to every corner of the world.

chapters.title: The Archosaurs
chapters.tease: One Triassic family split in two, and one branch led through dinosaurs to every bird alive today.

chapters.title: The Crocodile-Line Rulers
chapters.tease: For thirty million years the crocodile line, not the dinosaurs, ruled the Triassic land.

chapters.title: Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus
chapters.tease: Two Argentine finds showed that the very first dinosaurs were small, rare and already splitting into lineages.

chapters.title: Hunting for the First Dinosaur
chapters.tease: Tracks and bones from five countries have narrowed the dinosaurs' birth to southern Pangaea, 245–233 mya.

chapters.title: Coelophysis at Ghost Ranch
chapters.tease: One mass grave of hundreds of Coelophysis made it among the best-known early dinosaurs.

chapters.title: Plateosaurus and the Early Long-Necks
chapters.tease: Plateosaurus showed how the long-necked body plan of the giant sauropods began, in Triassic Europe.

chapters.title: The Carnian Pluvial Episode
chapters.tease: A million rainy years 233 million years ago helped dinosaurs spread and reshaped life on land and sea.

chapters.title: The End-Triassic Extinction
chapters.tease: Volcanoes that split Pangaea wiped out the dinosaurs' rivals and opened the Jurassic to them.

chapters.title: Sauropods: Life at Full Stretch
chapters.tease: Sauropods showed how far evolution could push a land animal: 140 million years of giants on every continent.

chapters.title: Diplodocus
chapters.tease: Diplodocus became the world's most familiar dinosaur and the yardstick for every long-necked giant.

chapters.title: Brachiosaurus and Giraffatitan
chapters.tease: These giraffe-shaped giants showed sauropods could browse treetops, and that one famous name can hide two animals.

chapters.title: Brontosaurus Returns
chapters.tease: Brontosaurus showed that a name is a hypothesis: sunk in 1903, it was revived by a data-driven family tree in 2015.

chapters.title: Argentinosaurus and the Titanosaurs
chapters.tease: The titanosaurs produced the heaviest land animals ever and were still flourishing when the asteroid struck.

chapters.title: How Big Could They Get?
chapters.tease: Weighing sauropods turned palaeontology into a science of method, and set the known limit for land animals.

chapters.title: Air Sacs and Hollow Bones
chapters.tease: Sauropods breathed like birds, with air sacs that hollowed their bones and made giant necks possible.

chapters.title: Mamenchisaurus and the Longest Necks
chapters.tease: Mamenchisaurus grew the longest neck of any known animal, about 15 m, more than seven times a giraffe's.

chapters.title: Auca Mahuevo: A Sauropod Nesting Ground
chapters.tease: Auca Mahuevo gave us the first sauropod embryos and proof that titanosaurs nested in colonies for generations.

chapters.title: Dippy and the Museum Giants
chapters.tease: Carnegie's plaster casts made Diplodocus the most widely seen dinosaur on Earth and museum giants a global habit.

chapters.title: A Greenhouse Planet Splits Apart
chapters.tease: The break-up of Pangaea split one dinosaur world into many and built the oceans we sail today.

chapters.title: The Morrison Formation
chapters.tease: One rock formation in the American West gave the world Diplodocus, Allosaurus and Stegosaurus.

chapters.title: Allosaurus
chapters.tease: The best-known big Jurassic predator, studied from dozens of skeletons rather than one lucky find.

chapters.title: Stegosaurus
chapters.tease: Its plates and tail spikes made it an icon; one near-complete skeleton made it a testable animal.

chapters.title: Scelidosaurus and the First Armour
chapters.tease: The first nearly complete dinosaur skeleton ever found showed how dinosaur armour began.

chapters.title: Cryolophosaurus: Antarctica's Crested Hunter
chapters.tease: A crested predator found 4,000 m up an Antarctic peak proved dinosaurs thrived near the poles.

chapters.title: Guanlong and the Early Tyrannosaurs
chapters.tease: T. rex's family started as small, crested hunters; Guanlong shows where the giants came from.

chapters.title: The Solnhofen Lagoon
chapters.tease: A poisoned lagoon in Bavaria preserved feathers, wings and footprints in stone fine enough to print with.

chapters.title: Archaeopteryx
chapters.tease: A feathered skeleton found in 1861 gave Darwin his missing link and birds their dinosaur ancestry.

chapters.title: The Trackways of Skye
chapters.tease: Footprints on Skye's shore reveal Middle Jurassic dinosaurs, a time whose bones are rare worldwide.

chapters.title: What Makes a Theropod?
chapters.tease: The two-legged dinosaur body plan that produced T. rex, Spinosaurus and every bird alive today.

chapters.title: Tyrannosaurus rex
chapters.tease: The last and largest tyrannosaur, now known as a fast-growing, keen-eyed, mostly scaly animal.

chapters.title: Sue, Stan and the Famous Rexes
chapters.tease: Over 30 skeletons made T. rex a population we can compare, not a single specimen to guess from.

chapters.title: Spinosaurus: The River Monster
chapters.tease: The longest predatory dinosaur, a fish-eater whose lifestyle is still one of palaeontology's liveliest arguments.

chapters.title: Giganotosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus
chapters.tease: Southern giants that rivalled T. rex in size, with slicing teeth built for sauropod-sized prey.

chapters.title: Baryonyx: The Fish-Eater from Surrey
chapters.tease: An amateur's claw find that revealed a whole family of crocodile-snouted, fish-eating predators.

chapters.title: Carnotaurus and the Abelisaurs
chapters.tease: The short-faced, nearly armless predators that ruled the southern continents while tyrannosaurs held the north.

chapters.title: Therizinosaurus: The Scythe Lizard
chapters.tease: A theropod that gave up meat for leaves, with the longest claws of any known animal.

chapters.title: How Fast Could T. rex Run?
chapters.tease: Biomechanics turned a film chase into testable physics, and cut T. rex's top speed to a jog.

chapters.title: Bite Force and the Hunt
chapters.tease: The strongest bite of any land animal, proven by bitten bones, healed wounds and fossil dung.

chapters.title: Ankylosaurus and the Tail Club
chapters.tease: A living tank with a bone club for a tail: proof that plant-eaters evolved weapons of their own.

chapters.title: Borealopelta: The Dinosaur Mummy
chapters.tease: The best-preserved armoured dinosaur ever found keeps its skin, its colour and its final meal.

chapters.title: Triceratops
chapters.tease: The commonest giant of the last dinosaur world, and the clearest case of how a dinosaur grew up.

chapters.title: Protoceratops and the Griffin Legend
chapters.tease: A beaked, four-legged skull from the gold-bearing Gobi may have helped inspire the griffin.

chapters.title: Styracosaurus and the Frill Puzzle
chapters.tease: Its spiked frill was too thin to stop a bite, so why grow it? The answer rewrote dinosaur behaviour.

chapters.title: The Fighting Dinosaurs
chapters.tease: The only fossil of two dinosaurs fighting at the moment of death, frozen in sand for 70 million years.

chapters.title: Pachycephalosaurus
chapters.tease: The thickest skull roof of any dinosaur, and the scars to prove it was used in battle.

chapters.title: Psittacosaurus and the Colour of Camouflage
chapters.tease: The first dinosaur whose camouflage was measured and tested, revealing the forest it hid in.

chapters.title: Showing Off: Crests, Frills and Display
chapters.tease: Crests, frills and colourful feathers turned the Mesozoic into a stage for courtship and rivalry.

chapters.title: The Centrosaurus Bonebeds
chapters.tease: A whole herd drowned in one flood, turning a single species into a population we can count.

chapters.title: Iguanodon and the Thumb Spike
chapters.tease: A spike first placed on the nose turned out to be a thumb, and Iguanodon's whole posture changed with it.

chapters.title: The Duck-Billed Dinosaurs
chapters.tease: The commonest big dinosaurs of the Late Cretaceous, and the ones that taught us how dinosaur populations lived.

chapters.title: Parasaurolophus and the Trumpet Crest
chapters.tease: A dinosaur with a built-in trumpet: CT scans let us hear, roughly, what a duck-bill sounded like.

chapters.title: Maiasaura: The Good Mother Lizard
chapters.tease: The nest site that put dinosaur families, colonies and parental care into the textbooks.

chapters.title: Edmontosaurus and the Dinosaur Mummies
chapters.tease: Skin, crests and hooves preserved as impressions turned a familiar skeleton into a fleshed-out animal.

chapters.title: Dental Batteries: The Best Chewers Ever
chapters.tease: Hundreds of teeth in self-renewing columns made hadrosaurs some of the most efficient plant-chewers in history.

chapters.title: Polar Dinosaurs
chapters.tease: Dinosaurs nested and raised young through months of polar darkness, undermining the cold-blooded reptile image.

chapters.title: Herds on the Move
chapters.tease: Bonebeds, trackways, nesting grounds and isotopes now make dinosaur herds a fact rather than a painting.

chapters.title: Growing Up Dinosaur
chapters.tease: Growth rings in bone and teeth reveal incubation times, teenage growth spurts and dinosaurs breeding young.

chapters.title: Hypsilophodon and the Small Sprinters
chapters.tease: Small, fast and overlooked, these ornithopods lasted 100 million years and taught us dinosaurs could run and burrow.

chapters.title: Sinosauropteryx: The First Feathered Dinosaur
chapters.tease: The first non-bird dinosaur found with a coat of feathers, and later the first whose colours could be read.

chapters.title: The Jehol Biota
chapters.tease: Volcanic lakes in north-east China preserved a whole Cretaceous ecosystem, feathers, fur and flowers included.

chapters.title: Velociraptor: Myth and Reality
chapters.tease: The film star was a feathered, turkey-sized desert hunter, more bird of prey than scaly monster.

chapters.title: Deinonychus and the Dinosaur Renaissance
chapters.tease: One claw from Montana turned dinosaurs from sluggish failures into active, bird-like animals.

chapters.title: Microraptor: Four Wings
chapters.tease: A dinosaur with four wings and iridescent black plumage, proof that flight was an experiment with many attempts.

chapters.title: Yutyrannus: A Feathered Tyrant
chapters.tease: A 9-metre feathered tyrannosauroid showed that even big predators could wear a coat.

chapters.title: Oviraptor: Wrongly Accused
chapters.tease: The 'egg thief' was really a parent: proof that dinosaurs brooded their nests like birds.

chapters.title: Dinosaur Colours Revealed
chapters.tease: Microscopic pigment capsules turned dinosaur colour from guesswork into evidence.

chapters.title: Brains, Senses and Clever Dinosaurs
chapters.tease: CT scans of braincases show dinosaurs could smell, see and hear far better than the pea-brain myth suggests.

chapters.title: From Dinosaur to Bird
chapters.tease: Birds were built from dinosaurs piece by piece, so the dinosaurs never entirely died out.

chapters.title: Pterosaurs: Masters of the Air
chapters.tease: The first vertebrates to fly, on wings of skin stretched from a single giant finger, for 150 million years.

chapters.title: Quetzalcoatlus
chapters.tease: The size limit of flight: a pterosaur as tall as a giraffe, with the wingspan of a light aircraft.

chapters.title: Ichthyosaurs
chapters.tease: Reptiles that turned into dolphins: warm-blooded, live-bearing ocean hunters for 150 million years.

chapters.title: Plesiosaurs
chapters.tease: Four-flippered sea reptiles in two plans: the absurdly long neck, or the giant head with crushing jaws.

chapters.title: Mosasaurs
chapters.tease: Giant sea-going lizards that ruled the last Cretaceous oceans, and helped prove that extinction is real.

chapters.title: Mammals in the Shadows
chapters.tease: Mammals lived beside dinosaurs for 140 million years, and not all of them were shrews.

chapters.title: Crocodile Cousins: Sarcosuchus and Deinosuchus
chapters.tease: Crocodile relatives longer than a bus, big enough to ambush dinosaurs at the water's edge.

chapters.title: Flowering Plants Arrive
chapters.tease: In about 40 million years, flowering plants went from rare weeds to the plants that run the land.

chapters.title: Insects, Pollinators and Amber
chapters.tease: Insects invented pollination alongside the dinosaurs, and amber caught them in the act.

chapters.title: Hell Creek: The Last Dinosaur World
chapters.tease: The best-recorded snapshot of the very last dinosaur world, right up to the clay layer that ended it.

chapters.title: The Chicxulub Impact
chapters.tease: A 10 km asteroid hit Yucatán 66 million years ago and ended the age of dinosaurs in a single day.

chapters.title: The Alvarez Hypothesis
chapters.tease: A clock experiment found too much iridium, and turned dinosaur extinction into a question for physics.

chapters.title: The Deccan Traps
chapters.tease: Lava a million cubic kilometres in volume erupted as the dinosaurs died. Was it a rival killer or an accomplice?

chapters.title: Tanis: The Day the Sky Fell
chapters.tease: Fish breathed in impact glass minutes after Chicxulub. Tanis may record the end of the dinosaurs minute by minute.

chapters.title: Who Survived, and Why
chapters.tease: Size, diet and shelter decided who crossed the boundary, and so who would inherit the planet.

chapters.title: Birds: The Living Dinosaurs
chapters.tease: Birds are theropod dinosaurs, and with around 11,000 species they outnumber mammals almost two to one.

chapters.title: Dinosaurs on Screen
chapters.tease: Screen dinosaurs shape what the public believes, and every era gets the dinosaurs its science allows.

chapters.title: Could We Bring Them Back?
chapters.tease: DNA falls apart far too quickly to survive 66 million years, which leaves only one route: rewind a bird.

chapters.title: The Golden Age of Discovery
chapters.tease: Around one new dinosaur species is named every week, most of them in places barely explored a century ago.

chapters.title: What Dinosaurs Teach Us About Our Future
chapters.tease: Dinosaurs ruled for 165 million years. Their end shows how fast worlds break and how slowly they mend.
